tagline.text: The island-tour starting beach where the sun sets between Capones and Camara islands

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half a day to 2 days and 1 night

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱2,500–4,500 (per person, based on an island tour with a boat shared by 4)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Clark International Airport (CRK) or Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL)

children.text: Pundaquit is a coastal village in San Antonio, Zambales, and the place where boats leave for Anawangin, Nagsasa and Silanguin coves and Capones Island. Its gray volcanic ash sand and the sunset between two islands are worth seeing, and you can plan a day trip from Manila by bus.

Pundaquit is a barangay and beach village in the municipality of San Antonio, Zambales. San Antonio is a small town on the Olongapo–Bugallon road, about 167 km from Manila and about 48 km from the provincial capital Iba, and it had a population of about 38,000 in the 2024 census. Its coastline is lined with gray volcanic-ash coves and islands, and almost all of the boat tours to them leave from Pundaquit Beach. For travelers, then, Pundaquit is less a destination than a gateway. During the day it feels like a boat landing where the boat owners (bangkeros) wait for customers, and few people come just for the beach itself.

Still, the beach has a real charm of its own. Its sand is a fine gray, shaped by the volcanic ash that settled during the 1991 Mount Pinatubo eruption, and it looks brighter once it dries. The best-known scene is the sunset. Many travel guides say that from the beach, looking west over the sea, you can watch the sun sink between the silhouettes of Capones Island and Camara Island. In the late afternoon, after the boat customers have gone, the beach is relatively quiet and pleasant for a walk or for waiting out the evening. Small resorts, guesthouses and eateries line the shore, and many visitors stay here the night before an island tour.

About 10 minutes by boat from Pundaquit stands the Capones Island lighthouse, built in 1890. Built in the last years of Spanish colonial rule, it guided ships to and from Subic Bay and Corregidor, and it now serves as a navigation aid with a solar-powered light. You have to climb stairs up from the landing and the ascent is steep, but from the top you get a sweeping view of Capones and Camara islands and the Pundaquit shoreline. The most common plan is a one-day trip that combines Camara Island and Anawangin, Nagsasa and Silanguin coves on the same boat. Each of these coves has its own entry, so read those as well.

Pundaquit also has an arts story. In Barangay San Miguel in San Antonio stands Casa San Miguel, an arts center founded in 1993 by the violinist Alfonso "Coke" Bolipata. Set in the middle of a mango orchard, it teaches music and art to local children and holds events every year such as the Pundaquit Festival and the Zambulat arts and music festival. If the schedule works out, catching a performance or exhibition adds a nice experience to a beach trip. This guide is written for travelers who go from Manila to Pundaquit for a day or for 2 days and 1 night to do an island tour. Boat fares and entrance fees change from year to year and differ between sources, so check the latest rates with the San Antonio tourism office or your boat operator before you go.

blocks.title: Sunset between Capones and Camara islands

children.text: This is why Pundaquit Beach is most famous. People say you can watch the sun set between Capones Island and Camara Island, out in the western sea. It helps to find a spot on the beach around
(this varies by season). Cloudy days give weaker colors, so consider staying overnight to allow some flexibility.

This Spanish-era lighthouse was first lit in 1890. You climb stairs partway up the hillside from the landing, and together with the lighthouse stairs it takes real effort. From the top you can see Camara Island and Pundaquit Beach at a glance. Whether the lighthouse is open and which parts you can climb may vary over time, so ask your boat operator.
This rocky island sits across from Capones Island and is a good stop on the way back. It has almost no facilities, so a day visit is the norm. Bring snorkeling gear, water and snacks with you.

blocks.title: Boat tours to Anawangin, Nagsasa and Silanguin coves

children.text: Many guides give the boat ride from Pundaquit to Anawangin Cove as about
20 minutes
and to Nagsasa Cove as about
1 hour
. Silanguin is the farthest cove. Each cove differs in sand color and atmosphere, so tours that combine two or three in a day are common.

This arts center sits in a mango orchard in Barangay San Miguel and was founded in 1993 by Alfonso Bolipata. It is known for its youth orchestra, the Pundaquit Virtuosi, and for its education programs for local students, and it holds music and art events every year. Check on site for the hours when visitors are welcome.
A trail leads from Pundaquit over the mountain to Anawangin Cove. One travel blog said it takes about
4–5 hours
. There is little shade and the path is easy to lose, so going with a local guide is safer, and the boat is far easier.

Some Pundaquit boat owners run fishing tours separately and will prepare fishing gear if you tell them in advance. Travelers say the stars show up well when you look up at the low-light sky from a cove or the beach at night.

items.title: Day trip
items.subtitle: An island tour with an early start from Manila

children.text: Take a bus to Iba from a Victory Liner terminal in Manila (Sampaloc, Cubao, Pasay, Caloocan and so on). Get off in front of the San Antonio market.
Take a tricycle from the San Antonio market to the Pundaquit landing. On arrival, pay the environmental fee and settle on a boat.
Take the boat to Capones Island. Climb the lighthouse stairs for the view, then continue via Camara Island to the coves.
Eat a packed lunch or a meal at a local eatery on the cove beach, and swim.
Return to Pundaquit, shower and rest, then watch the sunset.
Take a tricycle into San Antonio, check the time of the last bus to Manila, and board.
A day trip is tight because of the long travel time. If you can, arrive the night before and take a boat the next morning for a more relaxed pace.
Arrive in Pundaquit, drop your bags at your lodging, and walk the beach to see the sunset.
Eat dinner at your lodging or a village eatery and turn in early.
Take a boat early in the morning and tour Capones and Camara islands and the coves.
After lunch return to Pundaquit, shower, go out to San Antonio and board a bus toward Manila.
If you want to see nearby Casa San Miguel, make a short visit on the afternoon or early morning of the second day.
Take a Victory Liner bus to Iba. Routes leave from the Sampaloc, Cubao, Pasay and Caloocan terminals, and one travel guide put the fare at about ₱360 (fares change).
Get off in front of the San Antonio Public Market. Many guides say it takes about
4–5 hours
from Manila.
Tricycles run from the market to Pundaquit. The fare is ₱30–40 per person, and a special trip costs more.
Bus fares vary widely by source, from ₱250 to ₱400. Check the current fare at the terminal.
Enter "Pundaquit Beach" in Google Maps or Waze and it will guide you there.
The usual route is via NLEX and SCTEX and then down the Zambales coastal road. The travel time varies a lot with traffic, so allow plenty of time.
Parking at resorts and in the village near the landing is limited, so check parking with your lodging in advance.

items.title: Getting around the village and by boat

children.text: From the landing the boat ride takes about
10 minutes
to Capones Island and about
20 minutes
to Anawangin Cove.
Within San Antonio, tricycles are the main way to get around.
Pundaquit is best in the dry season from November to May. The seas are calm and boats run reliably. In the rainy season waves get rough and boat service can be limited.

San Antonio receives about 1,280 mm of rain a year, concentrated from June to September. March to May is very hot, so a hat and sunscreen are essential. Weekends and holidays are crowded at the coves and the landing, so weekdays are much more relaxed.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Good for both boats and sunsets, but crowded on weekends and around New Year.
The sea is calm and the sun is strong. Bring plenty of shade and water.
Some days no boats go out. Leave some slack in your schedule.

There are many small beach resorts around Pundaquit. Lodgings around San Antonio that have been mentioned include Youhan Beach Resort, The Penta Beach Resort, Funtasea Hotel and Beach Resort, Bom Dia Hostel, White Castle Beach Resort, Megans Paradisio Beach Resort, Playa Alba and The Palms Resort & Bar. Rates and operating status change with the season, so check before booking.

You eat at your lodging or at village eateries. Many coves have almost nowhere to buy food, so buy packed meals, water and snacks in Pundaquit or at the San Antonio market in advance. Many travelers also pick up Filipino snacks (kakanin) at the San Antonio market.
Staying one night rather than making a day trip lets you catch both the sunset and a morning boat, which is far more relaxed.
Boat fares are often quoted per boat, so split the cost by the number of people. Booking ahead is safer in peak season and on weekends.
Islands and coves have few places to eat, so bring lunch, water and snacks and carry your trash back out.
Use reef-safe sunscreen (free of oxybenzone and similar ingredients) and a reusable water bottle.
The sunset is seen best from the beach, so claim a spot about 30 minutes before sundown.
If you plan to visit Casa San Miguel, check its visiting hours and event schedule first.
In the rainy season (June–October) and during typhoons, waves can be too rough for boats to go out. Check the weather and whether boats are running before you leave.
Keep to the boat's passenger limit and always wear a life jacket.
Mobile signal can be poor at remote coves. Save emergency contacts in advance.
Fees and rates vary a lot from one article to the next, so confirm exact amounts on site.
The Capones lighthouse stairs can be steep and slippery, so wear sneakers rather than sandals.
